## 1. Macaroons (Birgisson, Politz, Erlingsson, Taly, Vrable, Lentczner — NDSS 2014)

Primary source: the paper PDF at
<http://theory.stanford.edu/~ataly/Papers/macaroons.pdf> (Google Research listing:
<https://research.google/pubs/macaroons-cookies-with-contextual-caveats-for-decentralized-authorization-in-the-cloud/>;
NDSS 2014 programme entry:
<https://www.ndss-symposium.org/ndss2014/ndss-2014-programme/macaroons-cookies-contextual-caveats-decentralized-authorization-cloud/>).
I fetched the PDF and extracted its text locally, so the quotes below are first-hand from
the paper body.

### 1.1 The shape matches ours closely

The abstract states macaroons are "bearer credentials, like Web cookies," but that
"macaroons embed caveats that attenuate and contextually confine when, where, by who, and
for what purpose a target service should authorize requests." That is exactly our shape:
the restriction travels inside the credential, and the *target service* (our egress proxy)
enforces it.

Mechanism: a macaroon is a chain of nested HMACs. From the paper: "Fundamental to this
flexibility of macaroons is a chained construction of nested HMAC values that
simultaneously provides key distribution and protects integrity, generalizing earlier work
dating back to the Amoeba operating system." The target service holds a root key `K_TS`
and can "compute and verify the terminal, derived HMAC value, even when the resulting
macaroon is further attenuated with a caveat." Note this is symmetric-key HMAC, not
public-key signing as in our sketch — a difference in cryptography, not in architecture.

### 1.2 Attenuation is monotonic (only narrows)

Confirmed. Caveats are "predicates that restrict the macaroon's authority, as well as the
context in which it may be successfully used." A derived macaroon is described as "a strict
attenuation of another, more permissive macaroon." The construction enforces this
cryptographically: because each caveat is folded into the HMAC chain, and the holder only
knows the *terminal* signature (not the root key), a holder can append caveats (producing a
new valid signature) but cannot remove one — removing a caveat would require recomputing
the chain from a key it does not have. Fig. 1's caption in the paper: "By attenuating a
macaroon authorizing O, a derived macaroon may permit access only to o3."

This is the property our design depends on if we ever let a session hand a further-narrowed
token to a sub-agent. **Precedent is solid and 12+ years old.**

### 1.3 Third-party caveats and discharge macaroons

A third-party caveat requires the bearer to present an *additional* macaroon (a "discharge
macaroon") issued by some other service, proving a condition. Per the paper, to authorize a
request the target service verifies "(i) that caveat discharge macaroons can be found for
all third-party caveats, and (ii) that all first-party caveats" hold. Example from the
paper: a forum service FS derives a macaroon for user "bob" that attenuates what is
accessible while simultaneously delegating *authentication* of the user to a third-party
service.

Important for us: a third-party caveat is exactly the "call back to the control plane"
that our design is trying to avoid — except the callback is made by the **client**, ahead
of time, not by the enforcing proxy on the hot path. The client gathers fresh discharge
macaroons and presents them with the request. That is a materially different cost
structure from the proxy doing a synchronous lookup, and it is worth noting as a design
option: *push* the freshness proof to the caller rather than *pull* it at the enforcer.

### 1.4 How macaroons actually handle revocation — the key finding

The paper does **not** claim to solve revocation. It explicitly names it a long-standing
open problem and then enumerates the standard mitigations. Direct quote (Section II):

> "In particular, revocation of authority is a long-standing challenge for
> credentials-based authorization systems... Broadly, this challenge has been addressed by
> (i) using very short-lived credentials, (ii) allowing the addition of freshness
> constraints, (iii) relying on external, authoritative state (such as revocation lists, or
> epoch counters), and (iv) splitting credentials, and granting authority only to a
> freshly-gathered collection. Macaroons excel at all four of these revocation strategies:
> due to their efficiency, and flexibility, macaroons may live only for seconds, and may be
> split or constrained in any manner."

Note the careful framing: macaroons are good at *hosting* the four mitigations; they do not
remove the need for one. Section V.E ("Revocation and Versioning") repeats this: revocation
"may be done via a database 'whitelist' (resp. 'blacklist') of valid macaroons (resp.
invalid), via embedding expiry times or epoch counters in macaroons, or via some
combination of the above."

Three more first-hand details worth having:

- **Seconds-scale TTLs are the paper's own headline answer.** "macaroons may live only for
  seconds." In the cookie-replacement example the paper describes binding "to a single
  client IP address, and a validity period of only a few seconds."
- **Revocation via a third-party caveat means the *client* re-fetches a discharge**, and
  the paper says that discharge "can, and should, be very short lived." It also notes an
  efficiency trick: many macaroons can share one revocation-check caveat, so "a single
  macaroon can discharge that caveat for any image" — i.e. one fresh discharge amortizes
  over hundreds of credentials.
- **The opaque-identifier alternative trades statelessness away.** The paper notes you can
  index by a random nonce, which makes "revocation to be simply done by deleting a database
  row; however, the downside is that the target must maintain a database, either centralized
  or replicated across the servers operating the service." This is precisely our tradeoff,
  stated in the primary source.

There is also a case we should copy: revocation is needed "when target services are
updated" — e.g. a `delete` operation is added to a previously read-only service and
existing macaroons don't constrain operations. The paper's answer is a **default-deny
policy** for the new operation. Lesson for us: the proxy should default-deny models/
operations a token doesn't explicitly mention, so adding upstream capability doesn't
retroactively widen live tokens.

### 1.5 Comparison the paper draws to PKI

Relevant because our sketch uses public-key verification: the paper argues public-key
systems like SPKI/SDSI "are not truly decentralized, but instead require a
globally-accessible infrastructure, such as a revocation list, or a repository of
certificates," and that chain discovery can be costly (worst case cubic in repository size
for SPKI/SDSI). So the macaroon authors regard "needs a revocation list" as a *defect* they
are avoiding — by using short TTLs instead.

### 1.6 Fly.io / Tailscale real-world macaroon use — status

**NOT VERIFIED so far.** My web searches for Fly.io's macaroon token posts and Tailscale
macaroon usage returned no results in this environment (two queries, zero links). Fly.io
does publish a `macaroon` Go package and has written about their tokens publicly, but I
have not been able to reach a primary URL to cite, so I am not asserting anything about
their revocation approach. Flagging as a gap rather than guessing.

## 3. AWS STS: AssumeRole session policies (scope-down policies)

*(Taking these out of order — AWS is the most load-bearing precedent and the one with the
most explicit official language on revocation.)*

### 3.1 Session policies narrow only, and the effective permission is an intersection

Primary source: <https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access_policies.html#policies_session>

Verified quotes:

> "Session policies are advanced policies that you pass as a parameter when you
> programmatically create a temporary session for a role or an AWS STS federated user
> principal. **The permissions for a session are the intersection of the identity-based
> policies for the IAM entity (user or role) used to create the session and the session
> policies.** ... An explicit deny in any of these policies overrides the allow."

And from the policy-type summary on the same page:

> "Session policies limit the permissions that the role or user's identity-based policies
> grant to the session. **Session policies limit permissions for a created session, but do
> not grant permissions.**"

Concrete limits, verified: you pass one inline JSON session policy via the `Policy`
parameter, and up to **10 managed session policies** via `PolicyArns`. Applies to
`AssumeRole`, `AssumeRoleWithSAML`, and `AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity`.

This is the monotonic-narrowing property (macaroon attenuation) expressed in IAM's policy
language, and it is one of the most heavily used authorization mechanisms in the industry.
**Our "token can only narrow" assumption has extremely strong precedent.**

One caveat that matters if we ever mint sub-session tokens: a resource-based policy naming
the *session* ARN as principal is **not** limited by the session policy — "The resulting
session has all the permissions of the resource-based policy *plus* the intersection of the
identity-based policy and the session policy." So AWS's narrowing guarantee has a
documented escape hatch via resource-side grants. Analogue for us: if the *upstream
provider* or the proxy's own config grants something the token didn't mention, the token's
narrowing is bypassed. Keep the proxy default-deny.

Confirmed. Caveats are "predicates that restrict the macaroon's authority, as well as the
context in which it may be successfully used." A derived macaroon is described as "a strict
attenuation of another, more permissive macaroon." The construction enforces this
cryptographically: because each caveat is folded into the HMAC chain, and the holder only
knows the *terminal* signature (not the root key), a holder can append caveats (producing a
new valid signature) but cannot remove one — removing a caveat would require recomputing
the chain from a key it does not have. Fig. 1's caption in the paper: "By attenuating a
macaroon authorizing O, a derived macaroon may permit access only to o3."

This is the property our design depends on if we ever let a session hand a further-narrowed
token to a sub-agent. **Precedent is solid and 12+ years old.**

### 1.3 Third-party caveats and discharge macaroons

A third-party caveat requires the bearer to present an *additional* macaroon (a "discharge
macaroon") issued by some other service, proving a condition. Per the paper, to authorize a
request the target service verifies "(i) that caveat discharge macaroons can be found for
all third-party caveats, and (ii) that all first-party caveats" hold. Example from the
paper: a forum service FS derives a macaroon for user "bob" that attenuates what is
accessible while simultaneously delegating *authentication* of the user to a third-party
service.

Important for us: a third-party caveat is exactly the "call back to the control plane"
that our design is trying to avoid — except the callback is made by the **client**, ahead
of time, not by the enforcing proxy on the hot path. The client gathers fresh discharge
macaroons and presents them with the request. That is a materially different cost
structure from the proxy doing a synchronous lookup, and it is worth noting as a design
option: *push* the freshness proof to the caller rather than *pull* it at the enforcer.

### 1.4 How macaroons actually handle revocation — the key finding

The paper does **not** claim to solve revocation. It explicitly names it a long-standing
open problem and then enumerates the standard mitigations. Direct quote (Section II):

> "In particular, revocation of authority is a long-standing challenge for
> credentials-based authorization systems... Broadly, this challenge has been addressed by
> (i) using very short-lived credentials, (ii) allowing the addition of freshness
> constraints, (iii) relying on external, authoritative state (such as revocation lists, or
> epoch counters), and (iv) splitting credentials, and granting authority only to a
> freshly-gathered collection. Macaroons excel at all four of these revocation strategies:
> due to their efficiency, and flexibility, macaroons may live only for seconds, and may be
> split or constrained in any manner."

Note the careful framing: macaroons are good at *hosting* the four mitigations; they do not
remove the need for one. Section V.E ("Revocation and Versioning") repeats this: revocation
"may be done via a database 'whitelist' (resp. 'blacklist') of valid macaroons (resp.
invalid), via embedding expiry times or epoch counters in macaroons, or via some
combination of the above."

Three more first-hand details worth having:

- **Seconds-scale TTLs are the paper's own headline answer.** "macaroons may live only for
  seconds." In the cookie-replacement example the paper describes binding "to a single
  client IP address, and a validity period of only a few seconds."
- **Revocation via a third-party caveat means the *client* re-fetches a discharge**, and
  the paper says that discharge "can, and should, be very short lived." It also notes an
  efficiency trick: many macaroons can share one revocation-check caveat, so "a single
  macaroon can discharge that caveat for any image" — i.e. one fresh discharge amortizes
  over hundreds of credentials.

  index by a random nonce, which makes "revocation to be simply done by deleting a database

  or replicated across the servers operating the service." This is precisely our tradeoff,

updated" — e.g. a `delete` operation is added to a previously read-only service and
existing macaroons don't constrain operations. The paper's answer is a **default-deny
policy** for the new operation. Lesson for us: the proxy should default-deny models/
operations a token doesn't explicitly mention, so adding upstream capability doesn't
retroactively widen live tokens.

Relevant because our sketch uses public-key verification: the paper argues public-key
systems like SPKI/SDSI "are not truly decentralized, but instead require a
globally-accessible infrastructure, such as a revocation list, or a repository of
certificates," and that chain discovery can be costly (worst case cubic in repository size

> "Session policies are advanced policies that you pass as a parameter when you
> programmatically create a temporary session for a role or an AWS STS federated user
> principal. **The permissions for a session are the intersection of the identity-based
> policies for the IAM entity (user or role) used to create the session and the session
> policies.** ... An explicit deny in any of these policies overrides the allow."

And from the policy-type summary on the same page:

> "Session policies limit the permissions that the role or user's identity-based policies
> grant to the session. **Session policies limit permissions for a created session, but do
> not grant permissions.**"

Concrete limits, verified: you pass one inline JSON session policy via the `Policy`
parameter, and up to **10 managed session policies** via `PolicyArns`. Applies to
`AssumeRole`, `AssumeRoleWithSAML`, and `AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity`.

This is the monotonic-narrowing property (macaroon attenuation) expressed in IAM's policy
language, and it is one of the most heavily used authorization mechanisms in the industry.
**Our "token can only narrow" assumption has extremely strong precedent.**

One caveat that matters if we ever mint sub-session tokens: a resource-based policy naming
the *session* ARN as principal is **not** limited by the session policy — "The resulting
session has all the permissions of the resource-based policy *plus* the intersection of the
identity-based policy and the session policy." So AWS's narrowing guarantee has a
documented escape hatch via resource-side grants. Analogue for us: if the *upstream
provider* or the proxy's own config grants something the token didn't mention, the token's
narrowing is bypassed. Keep the proxy default-deny.

# Capability tokens: industrial precedents for embedding limits in the credential

Research question: we are considering having the platform mint, at session creation, a
capability token carrying `{tenant, session, model allowlist, spend cap, expiry}`, signed
with a platform key. The egress proxy (which holds the real upstream API keys) verifies
one public-key signature and **enforces whatever the token says**, never calling back to
the control plane. Goal: the proxy holds no tenant vocabulary and the hot path has no
control-plane dependency.

- **W1 — instant revocation is impossible** (a signed, self-contained token is valid
  until it expires).
- **W2 — cross-session cumulative quota needs a shared counter** (N concurrent tokens for
  one tenant cannot enforce a per-tenant total on their own).

**这是一个商业选择,不是架构公理** —— 决定它的是"token 账单记在谁的 provider 账户上"。
⇒ **"真 key 不进 guest"是转售形态才需要的性质**,本平台不承担;**BYO 在引擎侧是零加法**。**若前提反转(我们转售 key),整套设计不必重新发明** —— capability 凭证 · 中心
预扣额度 · per-tenant epoch 吊销 · token audience 绑定全部存档在 `_inbox/capability-tokens.md`。
**一条要诚实登记的**:**BYO 在同类平台是少数派**(七家一手核对在
`_inbox/peer-platform-credentials.md`),这条裁定不该被记成业界共识。

### 7.1 两条必须认领的代价

**① 没有第一方 token 计量。** `tokens_*` 只有在调用路径上的组件能诚实产出(`03 §9`),从
agent 事件解析是二手数据 ⇒ 我们不需要按 token 计费(provider 直接向租户开账单),但也**没有
成本看板、没有预算告警**。计量主干不受影响:两个产生点(沙箱生命周期、存储用量)恰好是记
**我们自己成本**的那两个;要做回来,补一个不持凭证的计量网关就够 —— **计量权不必靠持有凭证
获得。**

**② 租户自己的凭证暴露给 agent 生成的代码。** 沙箱里跑任意代码,所以 BYO 的准确表述不是
"key 是真的所以没事",而是"**租户用自己的凭证承担了这个暴露**"⇒ 可以接受,但应当是一句
**明示的产品声明**,不是默认沉默。**这条与 BYO 形态绑死,补任何组件都关不掉** —— 与 ① 不同
(① 补一个计量网关就能做回来)。

### 7.2 一条可检验的摆放规则:带凭证的文件只能落 per-Workspace 那一层

**判据是挂载基数,不是 volume 里装了什么**:一个 volume 若被多个 Workspace 共挂,共挂者看到
同一份字节 ⇒ **带凭证的文件住在那里就是结构性的跨租户凭证泄漏**,不是配置错是摆放错。

> **带凭证的文件(skill 里的 key、数据库连接串)只能落"只有一个 Workspace 能看到"的载体 ——
> Workspace volume(`§8.2`,一 Workspace 一个、`exclusive`)或沙箱 Overlay(`§8.3`);永不进
> 任何 shared 挂载的 volume。**

按基数表述比按用途强:不需要知道 volume 里装的是"知识"还是别的什么 ⇒ **可机械检验**(看挂载
行的基数,不看内容)。BYO 形态下这条就是多租户凭证安全的全部,是一条准入规则。
**粒度是 Workspace,不是 Tab** —— 同一个 Workspace 里各 Tab 的 agent 本来就共享文件面。

### 7.3 entitlement 与凭证无关,它仍然完整

控制面仍然拥有"这个租户能挂哪些 volume / 模板、能用哪条 DB 连接"—— 同一张授权表(`§10.1`)。
`model` 仍是注册表里的一种资源,含义是"**能用哪一份模型配置**(provider + base_url + 租户
自己的哪把凭证)",不是"能不能调某个模型" ⇒ **统一资源模型不依赖任何代理存在**。数据库侧
简化到底:直接是**租户自己的连接串**,连"部署 + 身份映射胶水"都不是。

### 7.4 域名级出网:一个极薄的「名字经纪」组件(用户裁定)

**引擎的出站声明只收 `{cidr, port, proto}`,而"只准 api.anthropic.com"这种收窄必须存在** ——
退到 IP / 端口挡不住任何东西(provider API 在 CDN 后面、IP 会漂)。**它落在平台侧的一个组件里,
而这不是引擎的缺陷**(K8s NetworkPolicy 同样只有 IP / CIDR)。形状是抄
Claude Code / Codex 已经在跑的那一种:
# Capability tokens: industrial precedents for embedding limits in the credential

Research question: we are considering having the platform mint, at session creation, a
capability token carrying `{tenant, session, model allowlist, spend cap, expiry}`, signed
with a platform key. The egress proxy (which holds the real upstream API keys) verifies
one public-key signature and **enforces whatever the token says**, never calling back to
the control plane. Goal: the proxy holds no tenant vocabulary and the hot path has no
control-plane dependency.

Two known weaknesses to test against precedent:
- **W1 — instant revocation is impossible** (a signed, self-contained token is valid
  until it expires).
- **W2 — cross-session cumulative quota needs a shared counter** (N concurrent tokens for
  one tenant cannot enforce a per-tenant total on their own).

Method: WebSearch + WebFetch of primary specs and official docs. Every claim below points
at a URL. Sections marked **NOT VERIFIED** are things I could not confirm first-hand.

---

## 1. Macaroons (Birgisson, Politz, Erlingsson, Taly, Vrable, Lentczner — NDSS 2014)

Primary source: the paper PDF at
<http://theory.stanford.edu/~ataly/Papers/macaroons.pdf> (Google Research listing:
<https://research.google/pubs/macaroons-cookies-with-contextual-caveats-for-decentralized-authorization-in-the-cloud/>;
NDSS 2014 programme entry:
<https://www.ndss-symposium.org/ndss2014/ndss-2014-programme/macaroons-cookies-contextual-caveats-decentralized-authorization-cloud/>).
I fetched the PDF and extracted its text locally, so the quotes below are first-hand from
the paper body.

### 1.1 The shape matches ours closely

The abstract states macaroons are "bearer credentials, like Web cookies," but that
"macaroons embed caveats that attenuate and contextually confine when, where, by who, and
for what purpose a target service should authorize requests." That is exactly our shape:
the restriction travels inside the credential, and the *target service* (our egress proxy)
enforces it.

Mechanism: a macaroon is a chain of nested HMACs. From the paper: "Fundamental to this
flexibility of macaroons is a chained construction of nested HMAC values that
simultaneously provides key distribution and protects integrity, generalizing earlier work
dating back to the Amoeba operating system." The target service holds a root key `K_TS`
and can "compute and verify the terminal, derived HMAC value, even when the resulting
macaroon is further attenuated with a caveat." Note this is symmetric-key HMAC, not
public-key signing as in our sketch — a difference in cryptography, not in architecture.

### 1.2 Attenuation is monotonic (only narrows)

Confirmed. Caveats are "predicates that restrict the macaroon's authority, as well as the
context in which it may be successfully used." A derived macaroon is described as "a strict
attenuation of another, more permissive macaroon." The construction enforces this
cryptographically: because each caveat is folded into the HMAC chain, and the holder only
knows the *terminal* signature (not the root key), a holder can append caveats (producing a
new valid signature) but cannot remove one — removing a caveat would require recomputing
the chain from a key it does not have. Fig. 1's caption in the paper: "By attenuating a
macaroon authorizing O, a derived macaroon may permit access only to o3."

This is the property our design depends on if we ever let a session hand a further-narrowed
token to a sub-agent. **Precedent is solid and 12+ years old.**

### 1.3 Third-party caveats and discharge macaroons

A third-party caveat requires the bearer to present an *additional* macaroon (a "discharge
macaroon") issued by some other service, proving a condition. Per the paper, to authorize a
request the target service verifies "(i) that caveat discharge macaroons can be found for
all third-party caveats, and (ii) that all first-party caveats" hold. Example from the
paper: a forum service FS derives a macaroon for user "bob" that attenuates what is
accessible while simultaneously delegating *authentication* of the user to a third-party
service.

Important for us: a third-party caveat is exactly the "call back to the control plane"
that our design is trying to avoid — except the callback is made by the **client**, ahead
of time, not by the enforcing proxy on the hot path. The client gathers fresh discharge
macaroons and presents them with the request. That is a materially different cost
structure from the proxy doing a synchronous lookup, and it is worth noting as a design
option: *push* the freshness proof to the caller rather than *pull* it at the enforcer.

### 1.4 How macaroons actually handle revocation — the key finding

The paper does **not** claim to solve revocation. It explicitly names it a long-standing
open problem and then enumerates the standard mitigations. Direct quote (Section II):

> "In particular, revocation of authority is a long-standing challenge for
> credentials-based authorization systems... Broadly, this challenge has been addressed by
> (i) using very short-lived credentials, (ii) allowing the addition of freshness
> constraints, (iii) relying on external, authoritative state (such as revocation lists, or
> epoch counters), and (iv) splitting credentials, and granting authority only to a
> freshly-gathered collection. Macaroons excel at all four of these revocation strategies:
> due to their efficiency, and flexibility, macaroons may live only for seconds, and may be
> split or constrained in any manner."

Note the careful framing: macaroons are good at *hosting* the four mitigations; they do not
remove the need for one. Section V.E ("Revocation and Versioning") repeats this: revocation
"may be done via a database 'whitelist' (resp. 'blacklist') of valid macaroons (resp.
invalid), via embedding expiry times or epoch counters in macaroons, or via some
combination of the above."

Three more first-hand details worth having:

- **Seconds-scale TTLs are the paper's own headline answer.** "macaroons may live only for
  seconds." In the cookie-replacement example the paper describes binding "to a single
  client IP address, and a validity period of only a few seconds."
- **Revocation via a third-party caveat means the *client* re-fetches a discharge**, and
  the paper says that discharge "can, and should, be very short lived." It also notes an
  efficiency trick: many macaroons can share one revocation-check caveat, so "a single
  macaroon can discharge that caveat for any image" — i.e. one fresh discharge amortizes
  over hundreds of credentials.
- **The opaque-identifier alternative trades statelessness away.** The paper notes you can
  index by a random nonce, which makes "revocation to be simply done by deleting a database
  row; however, the downside is that the target must maintain a database, either centralized
  or replicated across the servers operating the service." This is precisely our tradeoff,
  stated in the primary source.

There is also a case we should copy: revocation is needed "when target services are
updated" — e.g. a `delete` operation is added to a previously read-only service and
existing macaroons don't constrain operations. The paper's answer is a **default-deny
policy** for the new operation. Lesson for us: the proxy should default-deny models/
operations a token doesn't explicitly mention, so adding upstream capability doesn't
retroactively widen live tokens.

### 1.5 Comparison the paper draws to PKI

Relevant because our sketch uses public-key verification: the paper argues public-key
systems like SPKI/SDSI "are not truly decentralized, but instead require a
globally-accessible infrastructure, such as a revocation list, or a repository of
certificates," and that chain discovery can be costly (worst case cubic in repository size
for SPKI/SDSI). So the macaroon authors regard "needs a revocation list" as a *defect* they
are avoiding — by using short TTLs instead.

### 1.6 Fly.io / Tailscale real-world macaroon use — status

**NOT VERIFIED so far.** My web searches for Fly.io's macaroon token posts and Tailscale
macaroon usage returned no results in this environment (two queries, zero links). Fly.io
does publish a `macaroon` Go package and has written about their tokens publicly, but I
have not been able to reach a primary URL to cite, so I am not asserting anything about
their revocation approach. Flagging as a gap rather than guessing.

---

## 3. AWS STS: AssumeRole session policies (scope-down policies)

*(Taking these out of order — AWS is the most load-bearing precedent and the one with the
most explicit official language on revocation.)*

### 3.1 Session policies narrow only, and the effective permission is an intersection

Primary source: <https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access_policies.html#policies_session>

Verified quotes:

> "Session policies are advanced policies that you pass as a parameter when you
> programmatically create a temporary session for a role or an AWS STS federated user
> principal. **The permissions for a session are the intersection of the identity-based
> policies for the IAM entity (user or role) used to create the session and the session
> policies.** ... An explicit deny in any of these policies overrides the allow."

And from the policy-type summary on the same page:

> "Session policies limit the permissions that the role or user's identity-based policies
> grant to the session. **Session policies limit permissions for a created session, but do
> not grant permissions.**"

Concrete limits, verified: you pass one inline JSON session policy via the `Policy`
parameter, and up to **10 managed session policies** via `PolicyArns`. Applies to
`AssumeRole`, `AssumeRoleWithSAML`, and `AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity`.

This is the monotonic-narrowing property (macaroon attenuation) expressed in IAM's policy
language, and it is one of the most heavily used authorization mechanisms in the industry.
**Our "token can only narrow" assumption has extremely strong precedent.**

One caveat that matters if we ever mint sub-session tokens: a resource-based policy naming
the *session* ARN as principal is **not** limited by the session policy — "The resulting
session has all the permissions of the resource-based policy *plus* the intersection of the
identity-based policy and the session policy." So AWS's narrowing guarantee has a
documented escape hatch via resource-side grants. Analogue for us: if the *upstream
provider* or the proxy's own config grants something the token didn't mention, the token's
narrowing is bypassed. Keep the proxy default-deny.

### 3.2 Revocation — the official answer, verbatim
